stories.title: Rwanda genocide: Dutch court sentences man to life in prison
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5JZrB Over 800,00 people are estimated to have been murdered in the 1994 Rwandan genocide Image: DW Advertisement A Rwandan-born Dutch national was on Friday sentenced to life imprisonment by a court in the Netherlands for his role in the 1994 Rwandan genocide . The Hague District Court found that the 66-year-old man, identified only as Eugene N., had taken part in attacks on homes in Tutsi communities and thrown a grenade into a crowd of Tutsis sheltering in a football stadium, and convicted him of war crimes and genocide. "The conduct of the defendant establishes a significant lack of respect for human dignity and for human life," read a statement from the court issued after the conviction. "Only a lifelong prison sentence does justice to the immense suffering that has been inflicted on the victims and the bereaved families." Handing down the verdict, the presiding judge said N.'s actions were committed with "genocidal intent." Rwandan genocide: How many people died? During the 1994 genocide in Rwanda , more than 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus were killed in a campaign of mass murder orchestrated by Hutu extremists. Many leaders of the slaughter were tried and convicted by a United Nations war crimes tribunal that has now closed down. N. was sentenced for his role in the massacre of around 3,000 Tutsis in Mbazi in southern Rwanda in April 1994, in which prosecutors said he was "personally involved." "If the horrific crimes of the suspect, in which not one but an estimated 3,000 innocent people were literally slaughtered, in which the suspect personally threw a grenade into a stadium, do not deserve a life sentence, then what does?" one prosecutor asked the court.

stories.title: South Africa: Musina Residents Still Living With Sewage Despite Public Protector Findings
stories.summary: South Africa: Musina Residents Still Living With Sewage Despite Public Protector Findings 28 August 2026 Health-e (Cape Town) By Bernard Chiguvare Residents of Matswale township in Musina say persistent sewage spills and the stench from overflowing wastewater continue to disrupt their lives, more than a year after the Public Protector found that authorities had failed to properly maintain the town's sewage infrastructure. The report found that Vhembe District Municipality (VDM) and Musina Local Municipality (MLM) had failed to adequately address sewage spillages in Matswale Phase 10, Ward 5. The Public Protector also found that the resulting pollution and stench had violated residents' constitutional right to an environment that is not harmful to their health or wellbeing. The conduct of officials from both municipalities was found to constitute improper conduct and maladministration. More than a year later, residents in parts of Musina say they are still living with sewage flowing near their homes.

stories.summary: Benin: How Benin Is Turning Its Cotton Wealth Into An Industrial Economy Bird Story Agency GDIZ CEO, LÃ©tondji Beheton 28 August 2026 Bird Story Agency (Africa) By Ibrahim Oredola Falola Benin is using its position as West Africa’s largest cotton producer to pursue a bigger economic prize: processing more of what it grows at home. At the Glo-Djigbé Industrial Zone (GDIZ), cotton is being turned into fabrics and garments, creating jobs and retaining value that previously left the country with the trade of raw fibres. Its progress offers an emerging model for industrialisation for the continent. At the Glo-Djigbé Industrial Zone, about 45 kilometres north of Cotonou, young workers such as team leader Inès Alowakinnou are gaining experience in an industry that barely existed at this scale a few years ago. Their work lies at the centre of Benin’s ambitious attempt to turn its cotton wealth into factories, formal employment and a more diversified economy. “Working conditions are good, I’m gaining experience, and I wouldn’t hesitate to encourage any young person to follow my example,” says Alowakinnou, who works in the industrial engineering department.

The official results from the 13 August poll showed that incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema won with a 60% share of the vote compared to Mundubile's 38%. The day after the vote, security forces raided a property in the capital, Lusaka, linked to Mundubile, killing a former cabinet minister and arresting a number of other politicians. The authorities accused the opposition of planning an armed insurgency, which they denied. Following the raid, Mundubile went to a "secure location under the protection of an international human rights body due to threats made against him", his NRPUP party said.

stories.title: World's youngest reigning traditional monarch dies aged 34
stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, King Oyo ascended to the throne at the age of three but was crowned on reaching adulthood at 18 in 2010 By Swaibu Ibrahim BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Kampala Published 7 hours ago A traditional Ugandan ruler named as the world's youngest monarch has died aged 34, his prime minster announced. Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV became king of Tooro in western Uganda at just three years old in 1995 after the death of his father. The Tooro kingdom did not disclose the cause of King Oyo's death, but a Ugandan government minister was quoted in local media saying that he had been critically ill and was seeking treatment in the US. Though Uganda is governed by an elected president and parliament, it has several traditional kingdoms which continue to have significant cultural influence despite not having political power. Oyo, who Guinness World Records listed as the world's youngest reigning monarch , external , ruled over more than two million people.

La somme totale des rançons versées durant cette période aurait ainsi triplé par rapport à l'année précédente, passant de près de 2 millions de dollars à presque 6 millions de dollars transférés. « Les enlèvements de masse sont maintenant le mode opératoire dominant » La même tendance se dessine quant aux nombres de victimes : SBM Intelligence estime que 7 825 personnes ont été enlevées entre juin 2025 et fin-juin 2026, soit 66% de plus qu'à la même période l'année précédente. « Les enlèvements de masse sont maintenant le mode opératoire dominant », constatent les analystes.

"If you came out and started running, they shot you." The gunmen, who struck at 02:00, split into groups to surround residents: one at the village entrance, one in the centre and one at the back. "They opened fire without a care in the world, shooting indiscriminately," the 55-year-old quietly tells the BBC World Service. It was one of many attacks that have caused havoc in the mainly Muslim community where residents live in fear of being kidnapped for ransom. Fatima explains how the raids unfold: "You could have 100 motorcycles, and each one could be carrying three people." About 70 people, including children, were killed from the village of Bia Buki in June, according to Fatima. She describes how the attackers also targeted villagers as they fled and children were injured falling into ditches. Among the dead were her husband and six of his seven siblings.

stories.title: Did a goat herder's lucky $200 nugget spark a gold rush in western Kenya?
stories.summary: Image caption, Manasse Lomachar would like the discovery of gold to improve life in his village By Akisa Wandera Published 23 August 2026 A goat herder from a remote area of western Kenya has told the BBC his discovery of a golden nugget has sparked a gold rush, overwhelming his small village over the last few weeks. When people found out that 33-year-old Manasse Lomachar had sold his three grams of gold for 36,000 Kenyan shillings ($280; Â£205) several weeks ago, he believes this led to the arrival of thousands of prospectors in Cheporor. And it is true that what last month was just bushland and rough grazing ground near the village is now scarred by pits, mounds of earth and makeshift mining camps. It is not clear if was Lomachar's lucky find or other recent discoveries that sparked the excitement. But local authorities estimate that about 10,000 people arrived at the height of the rush.

stories.title: Ebola frontline workers missing wages as outbreak spreads ‘exponentially’
stories.summary: A health worker preparing to disinfect the area during the burial of suspected Ebola victims in Bunia. Photograph: Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/Reuters People fighting to contain rapidly growing outbreak in Democratic Republic of the Congo describe the obstacles and dangers they face By Prosper Heri Ngorora in Bunia and Rachel Savage E very day, Sophie Mwadawa Kabundo goes to her job as a nurse at an Ebola treatment centre in the north-east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo , afraid she will contract the virus and pass it to her family and friends. “More and more confirmed cases are being admitted here … Some of our colleagues have died,” said Kabundo. “We fear that, despite our vigilance, workplace accidents may occur and put us in ever greater danger … We go to sleep already worrying about the days ahead, as patients continue to pour in.” View image in fullscreen A health worker’s protective gear is disinfected after handling the body of a suspected Ebola victim in Bunia. Photograph: Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/Reuters Martin Bolombi, her colleague at the Elikya treatment centre in Bunia, the capital of the hardest-hit province, Ituri, holds similar fears. “Personally, this outbreak is causing me a lot of stress,” he said. “But I have no choice but to pluck up my courage and ensure that the situation is brought under control first, before it can stabilise.” Ebola outbreak: five big questions Read more That courage is all the more remarkable given that both workers on the frontline of the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record said they were not being paid. “I have been working since May and have only been paid for June,” said Bolombi, a hygiene worker who was among about 100 people who protested outside the Elikya treatment centre during a strike last month over unpaid bonuses. Kabundo said she was also missing wages. “We are not being paid and we want the government to provide solutions as soon as possible,” she said. “We are under immense pressure … We are exposed to the risk of infection, and our families and other loved ones may contract the disease because of us.” View image in fullscreen A health worker dries disinfected boots in Bunia. Photograph: Dieudonne Dirole/AP U npaid wages are just one of the factors – alongside misinformation, community mistrust and infrastructure deficits – hampering efforts to tackle the outbreak in the DRC, one of the world’s poorest countries.
